Choosing type for a design

Choose fonts that suit your project, test them with real content, and record how you’ll use them.

Based on Johnny’s reading notes, with explanations, resources, and ideas to explore. Updated October 21, 2026.

Explore the Choosing Type roadmap

PurposeAudienceInspirationFont selectionSizingStyle guideResourcesIdeas

1. Identify the purpose

Start by deciding what your readers need to learn or do. Someone visiting your portfolio might want to understand your role in a project. Someone attending a workshop might need to find its time and location. Use these needs to judge whether your typography helps them.

The medium is where the design will appear: a website, app, printed card, poster, or another format. Consider viewing distance, screen size, and how much text someone will read.

Decide how you want the design to feel. Lettering on a greeting card can complement its illustrations. On a page focused on photography, a less decorative font can leave more attention for the images. Consider typography alongside color, spacing, layout, and interaction.

Try it: Write the design’s purpose in 1 sentence, name where it will appear, and choose 2 words to describe how it should feel.

2. Identify the audience

Consider who will read your content and where they’ll use it. Think about their reading experience, interests, language, cultural context, device, and accessibility needs. Use what you know about your readers, and check assumptions with them when you can.

For people learning to read, check whether letter shapes are recognizable and similar characters are easy to tell apart. Sassoon Primary is an educational typeface you can explore in the resources below. If readers need larger text, check size, contrast, spacing, and how the layout behaves when they enlarge it. Test these choices together.

Try it: Describe a reader, what they need to find, and something that could make reading difficult.

3. Study examples

Choose a few designs to study. Look at their headings, paragraph widths, spacing, and font weights. Notice how the text works with the images. Before borrowing a choice, describe what it helps the reader see or understand.

Study font combinations as well as individual fonts. Which font is used for paragraphs? Which draws attention to headings? Check how the design separates these roles. Try the same content with 1 font family and then with 2.

Try it: Collect 3 examples and write a reason each is useful. Use what you notice to choose a few fonts to test.

4. Choose fonts and their roles

Legibility means how easily you can tell characters apart, such as a lowercase l and the number 1. Readability means how comfortably you can read the text as a whole. Check both with real titles, paragraphs, labels, and numbers from your project.

Some fonts are designed for large headings, long passages, or small interface labels. Read the designer’s description and look at their text samples, often called specimens. Then test the font at the size you plan to use. Decorative details may suit a short title and make a long paragraph harder to read.

Make the reading order clear

A font family is a related set of styles, such as regular, bold, and italic. You can use 1 family for both headings and paragraphs by changing its size, weight, or style. Try a second family if it helps distinguish their roles. This creates visual hierarchy: differences that help readers see what to read first.

The suggestion to use no more than 3 fonts is a guideline for keeping a design manageable. Choose each family for a reason. Regular, italic, and bold styles from the same family can provide variety without adding unrelated families.

Try it: Compare 3 fonts with the same content. Choose a treatment for headings and paragraphs, and explain why each fits.

5. Determine sizes and spacing

Choose a comfortable size for your paragraphs. A modular scale gives you related sizes to try. Start with a base size and multiply it by the same number, called a ratio, at each step. With a 16px base and a 1.25 ratio, the next sizes are 20px, 25px, and 31.25px.

Compare the gaps between sizes. Two ratios you’ll find in scale tools are the perfect fourth, about 1.333, and the golden ratio, about 1.618. A larger ratio creates bigger jumps. Use a scale as a starting point, then check whether its sizes fit your content and layout.

Choose the sizes you need and adjust them after viewing the page. Round values if that helps, or keep decimal values. Check line height, the space each line occupies, alongside paragraph width. On narrow and wide screens, check where headings wrap and whether captions remain comfortable to read.

Try it: Test 2 ratios with the same content. Keep the sizes that make the reading order clear, and adjust any that cause awkward wrapping.

6. Create a typography style guide

Record how you’ll use each text style so someone else can apply it consistently. Include its font family, size, weight, style, line height, letter spacing, color, and an example. Name a fallback font to use when the preferred font isn’t available. Note any changes needed for smaller screens.

Choose text colors that work with your palette and provide readable contrast against the background. Show where each style belongs. Save reusable text styles in your design software or in Cascading Style Sheets (CSS), which control how a web page looks.

Test the guide on real pages. If a choice makes the content harder to read or use, adjust it and update the guide.

Try it: Write down the styles for a title, paragraph, caption, and button label. Ask someone to apply them using your instructions.

Other references recorded in the notes

Creative Bloq’s free-font collection, Awwwards’ 2015 collection, InVision’s typography-resource collection, and the Behance Google Fonts Combinations volumes are recorded in the original article’s resource links. You’ll also find the original Mailchimp typography pattern and Focus Labs example there. These are older references, and some links may have changed.

For broader exploration, browse Behance and Dribbble. Sketch appears in the notes as an example of software with reusable text styles.

Find a font on a website: use your browser’s developer tools to inspect the page’s font styles. Identifying lettering in an image is a different task. The original reading uses “WhatTheFont” for a browser extension link, so check which task a tool supports before using it.

Ideas to explore

A guided font preference assessment

A short assessment could help you narrow your choices before browsing a font library. You’d answer questions about your project and compare examples. The tool would use your answers to suggest fonts and combinations to try.

Questions could ask you to rate a statement, choose between descriptions, or compare 2 visual examples. They could cover the project’s purpose, where it will appear, reading needs, desired mood, and your preferences for headings and paragraphs.

The tool would need a list of Google Fonts and system fonts with information about each. It could first check practical needs, such as language support, available styles, and which devices have a system font. It could then use your preferences to rank the remaining choices.

Each result should explain why the font fits and show it with real content. You should be able to see how both your project’s needs and your visual preferences shaped the suggestion. This feature is an idea for future work. We still need to decide what to measure, how much each answer matters, and how to assess combinations.

A typography comparison gallery

A comparison gallery could show website examples side by side. You could keep the content and layout the same, then change the fonts to see their effect. Compare the reading order, spacing, line breaks, and how the text works with images.

Questions for further study

What other elements communicate with users?
Explore imagery, color, layout, spacing, symbols, and motion alongside text.
How is a typeface’s intended use documented?
Read the designer’s description and text samples, then try the font in that role.
When does decorative type help?
Try the same decorative font in a short heading and a long paragraph. Notice where its details help or slow your reading.
When is one family enough?
Compare 1 family in different weights with 2 families assigned to headings and paragraphs.
